name: Matukar Panau
confidence_why: The quoted passage has not been checked against the cited source.
catalog_citation: Mansfield, John & Danielle Barth. 2021. Clause chaining and the utterance phrase: Syntax–prosody mapping in Matukar Panau. Open Linguistics 7: 423–447. doi:10.1515/opli-2021-0023 (Open Access, CC-BY; De Gruyter version of record, copy from ANU Open Research repository)
catalog_quote: Matukar Panau appears to have word stress, falling on the stem-final syllable of content words. Thus, for simple words we hear word-final stress, e.g. kalám “moon,” while for suffixed verbs we hear a word-internal stress, e.g. di-nagé-nggo “3P.S-put-I:R:IPFV.” While phonetic analysis of word stress is outside the scope of this study, its identification is facilitated by H* pitch accents that are anchored to these syllables, usually one per phonological phrase (see below). We tentatively analyse the stress domain, encompassing prefix and stem, as a “prosodic word” (ω). As is common for prosodic words (McCarthy and Prince 1993), this domain requires bimoraic minimal weight, evidenced by phonetic vowel lengthening in prosodic words that consist of a single open syllable. This can be observed both in simple words such as tiː “not,” and in verbs where the stem and prefix together consist of a single open syllable, e.g. ng-aː-gokai “1S.S-go-I:R:IPFV:HAB.” One or more prosodic words are encompassed by a “phonological phrase” (φ), in which one main content word has an H* pitch accent aligned to its stressed syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the stem of content words: word-final in unsuffixed words (kalám), but word-internal when suffixes follow (di-nagé-nggo), i.e. suffixes are outside the stress domain while prefixes are inside it (prosodic word = prefix + stem, right-edge stress). Monosyllabic open prosodic words lengthen to meet a bimoraic minimum (tiː 'not', ng-aː-gokai). Phrase-level H* pitch accent docks on the stressed syllable of the main content word of each phonological phrase.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; authors flag the analysis as tentative/impressionistic ('appears to have', 'we hear'), with no instrumental study of word stress; function words not covered (statement restricted to content words).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress identified auditorily in connected narrative speech and via alignment of H* phrasal pitch accents (one per phonological phrase); stress domain is the prosodic word = prefix+stem, excluding suffixes/enclitics. Language explicitly described as non-tonal (Barth et al. 2020).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Matukar Panau as spoken in Matukar and Surumarang villages (the whole language, glottocode matu1261); no dialect split. Note: the earlier scan's 'Barth, A Grammar of Matukar Panau (De Gruyter)' could not be verified to exist — no such grammar is cited in Mansfield & Barth 2021, Barth 2022, or Davey & Barth 2023, and Crossref/Semantic Scholar/ANU repository list none.

sources.note: p.434 §5.2: Matukar Panau 'appears to have word stress, falling on the stem-final syllable of content words' (kalám 'moon'; di-nagé-nggo with suffixes → word-internal stress); H* pitch accents anchor to the stressed syllable, one per phonological phrase; prosodic word = prefix+stem, bimoraic minimum with lengthening (tiː 'not'). Explicitly preliminary; no phonetic study of stress.
